title: 10 Tips for Motivating Students Toward Full Engagement in Pop-Up Debates https://davestuartjr.com/10-tips-for-motivating-students-toward-full-engagement-in-pop-up-debates/
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Dave Stuart Jr. walks through the ten moves he used to prepare and run a single pop-up debate on extreme poverty, his class's sixteenth of the year, tagging each move to the 'five key beliefs' (value, credibility, efficacy, effort, belonging) he tries to cultivate in students. The sequence runs from knowledge-building research and a prior check for understanding, through a write-and-share rehearsal warm-up and a visualization of why speaking skill matters, to data-based praise, an appeal to student ownership, coach-like interruptions, onscreen tracking, student choice of prompts, and a short post-game analysis. The point is not to copy the unit but to extract principles that transfer: rehearsal lowers risk, honest specific praise motivates, and fast feedback consolidates success. He stresses that none of the moves requires heavy planning, only repeated practice of a few core routines.
points: Rehearsing in writing and then with a partner before a debate means even a hesitant student called on cold has something prepared to say.
Praise works better when it is argued from evidence, such as telling a class they have done sixteen debates, than when it is vague encouragement.
Each routine is deliberately mapped onto one or more motivational beliefs, so the teacher can see why a move should raise engagement.
Teaching the research process first and shifting source evaluation onto students builds knowledge, choice, and efficacy before the discussion starts.
Closing with brief glows and grows from the argument notes delivers fast feedback and a last chance to build belief at a moment of success.
quotes: The point isn’t to stop praising students — it’s to think of giving praise as a kind of argumentation. When you praise a class or a student, you want to demonstrate, warmly but rationally, that the praise you’re giving is merited.

After five minutes of writing, I had them share what they wrote with their partners. Now, even if we get to a spot in the debate where I have to call on a hesitant student, the student will have had a chance to rehearse something twice: once in writing, once with a partner.

During the debate, I think of myself as the coach. I don’t want to interrupt so much that there’s no flow, but I also don’t want to let the argument get stuck like a broken record. If I see us getting stuck in one little corner of the playground, I’ll come in and model an argument that sets to rest that little corner of the argument.

Pop-up debates have always been for and about your future. We do this not just because it’s fun now, but because it’s so helpful to be able to speak well. But I need you to know why this matters to you.

But by this time in the year, there’s not much new I can teach you. Now, it’s up to you to push yourself as an arguer and a speaker. You know where you can improve. You know what it feels like to really try at something, and what it feels like to put in the minimum possible effort.

When we track each person’s contribution to the argument, we demonstrate that there are no “throwaway” speeches. I also think there’s something about note-taking that says to students, “Okay. This is important.
Many of the “moves” above are quick, and none of them require heavy pre-planning. All that I’ve done is studied and practiced six things, again and again, for years.
